mainTopic: The קנס for selling animals or slaves to a גוי, and how a גוי's partial ownership affects בכורה
overview: The גמרא first rejects a proof from a ברייתא that giving a גוי rights to an animal's future young is forbidden. The ברייתא is about an existing עובר, as its masculine word 'בדמיו' shows. In one version, ריש לקיש fines someone who sells a large animal to a גוי up to ten times its value. A slave's higher fine does not prove that 'ten' is loose, because a slave loses מצוות every day. In a second version the fine is one hundred times, and it is heavier than קבלנות because a sale cuts the animal off completely. The slave's smaller fine does not prove that 'one hundred' is loose, because selling a slave is uncommon, and the רבנן do not make decrees about uncommon cases. The גמרא then shows that רבי יהודה and the חכמים both build their views on the words ״כׇּל בְּכוֹר״, and it explains the verse in two ways. On how big a גוי's share must be to cancel בכורה, רב הונא says even an ear is enough. רב חסדא and רבא require a vital part, and they disagree about whether a טריפה can live. רב פפא rejects splitting the firstborn from the mother. The real reason for the exemption is mixed חולין ownership, not the animal's inability to live, as we see from נפלים. A story about רבי אלעזר and רבי אסי begins, and it continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Suggesting the ברייתא is about the mother animal
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that the ברייתא's ban refers to the animal itself. That would prove that giving a גוי rights to future offspring is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: Isn't the ברייתא talking about the animal itself?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to prove its question from the ברייתא it just quoted. It suggests that the ban there is about the mother animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the ברייתא is about a mother animal that is not yet pregnant, then it forbids giving a גוי a share in future offspring. That would answer the open question with a 'forbidden'. The phrase 'מאי לאו' signals that this is only a suggested reading, and it can still be pushed back.

keyTerms.meaning: Isn't it? A formula that offers a suggested reading in order to prove something
An animal (here, the mother animal itself)

phrases.english: What, is it not referring to the animal?
phrases.notes: The suggestion: the ברייתא's ban covers the mother animal, which would include rights to future young.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the attempt begun on the previous amud (2b) to settle, from a ברייתא, whether one may give a גוי rights to an animal's offspring.
steps.raayaObject: That giving a גוי rights to an animal's future offspring is forbidden
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא that forbids such arrangements and fines the seller up to ten times the value

steps.title: No, the ברייתא is about an existing fetus
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof. The ברייתא is about an animal that is already pregnant, so the ban is on selling an existing עובר.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is talking about the fetus.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back. The ברייתא is not about future offspring. It is about a fetus that already exists inside a pregnant animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Selling an existing עובר is forbidden, but that tells us nothing about offspring that do not exist yet. So the ברייתא no longer proves that selling rights to future offspring is forbidden. That question stays open, and it may well be allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: No. Opens a rejection of the suggested reading
A fetus; an unborn animal already inside its mother

phrases.english: No, it refers to the fetus.
phrases.notes: Meaning an existing fetus in an animal that is already pregnant, not future offspring.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the suggested proof of step 1 by narrowing the ברייתא's case.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the attempt to read the ברייתא as being about the mother animal and her future offspring
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא can be read as being about an already-existing עובר, so it proves nothing about future offspring
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up 'fetus' and 'future offspring.' An עובר here means a fetus that already exists in a pregnant animal. The open question is about young that have not even been conceived yet.

steps.title: The wording 'בדמיו' supports the fetus reading
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא says 'בדמיו' ('its value', masculine). That fits the עובר, not the mother animal, so the rejection is confirmed.
steps.simpleTranslation: The wording is also exact, because it teaches: 'They fine him up to ten times its (masculine) value.' Learn from this.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up the rejection from the ברייתא's own wording. The masculine word 'בדמיו' points to the fetus, so it agrees with the 'fetus' reading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word for animal, בהמה, is feminine, so the mother would be 'בדמיה'. The word עובר is masculine, which matches 'בדמיו'. 'שמע מינה' seals it: the ברייתא is about an existing fetus.

keyTerms.meaning: It is also precise. The wording itself supports this reading
Learn from it. Confirms the conclusion

phrases.english: It is also precise, as it teaches:
phrases.notes: Introduces support taken from the exact wording.

phrases.english: They penalize him up to ten times its value,
phrases.notes: 'בדמיו' is masculine, so it matches עובר (masculine), not בהמה (feminine).

phrases.english: Learn from it.
phrases.notes: The fetus reading is confirmed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the rejection in step 2 using grammar from the ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: That the ברייתא is about an existing עובר
steps.raayaSupportSource: The masculine form 'בדמיו' in the ברייתא
steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא forbids selling an existing עובר to a גוי. It does not prove that selling rights to future offspring is forbidden. The proof is the masculine word 'בדמיו'.

steps.title: The ברייתא supports ריש לקיש's ten-times fine
steps.stepSummary: The ten-times קנס in the ברייתא supports ריש לקיש. He rules that one who sells a large animal to a גוי is fined up to ten times its value.
steps.simpleTranslation: This supports ריש לקיש, who said: One who sells a large animal to a גוי is fined up to ten times its value.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא notes a side benefit of the ברייתא: it supports ריש לקיש's ruling on the size of the fine for selling a large animal to a גוי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sources use the same 'up to ten times the value' measure. So ריש לקיש's fine has backing from a ברייתא. Notice that ריש לקיש says 'בדמיה' (feminine), because he is talking about the animal itself.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא of ארץ ישראל, colleague of רבי יוחנן
A large animal (like a cow or donkey) that can be used for work
In its value (feminine form, referring to the animal)

phrases.english: This supports Reish Lakish,
phrases.notes: The support comes from the ten-times fine in the ברייתא.

phrases.english: as Reish Lakish says:
One who sells large livestock to a gentile —
phrases.notes: Selling a large animal to a גוי is forbidden by the חכמים.

phrases.english: they penalize him up to ten times its value.
phrases.notes: He must buy it back, even at up to ten times its price.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the ten-times fine from step 3 to support a separate statement of ריש לקיש.
steps.raayaObject: ריש לקיש's ruling: a ten-times fine for selling a large animal to a גוי
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא's fine of 'up to ten times its value'
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who sells a בהמה גסה to a גוי is fined up to ten times its value.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the standard size of the rabbinic קנס for selling a large animal to a גוי.

steps.title: Is 'ten times' an exact limit?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether 'up to ten times' is a fixed maximum or just an example.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is it exact, or not exact?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a clarifying question about ריש לקיש's number. Is ten the real ceiling, or could the fine go higher?
steps.deeperAnalysis: If 'ten' is דוקא, the fine can never pass ten times the value. If it is לאו דוקא, ten is just a way of saying 'a lot', and the fine could be bigger. This question sets up the next move.

phrases.english: Is it specifically so, or not specifically?
phrases.notes: Asks whether 'ten' is a true limit.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks how to understand the number in ריש לקיש's ruling.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether 'up to ten times its value' is an exact maximum

steps.title: רבי יהושע בן לוי fines up to one hundred times for a slave
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings רבי יהושע בן לוי, who fines a seller of a slave to a גוי up to one hundred times. This suggests that 'ten' is not exact.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: רבי יהושע בן לוי said: One who sells his slave to a גוי is fined up to one hundred times his value!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to answer the question with another statement. It shows a case where the fine reaches one hundred times, which would mean 'ten' is not a fixed limit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a fine can reach one hundred times, then the number in these fines does not seem to be a strict ceiling. That would make ריש לקיש's 'ten' לאו דוקא. The next step pushes back on this proof.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear. Introduces a source as a proof
A leading early אמורא of ארץ ישראל

phrases.aramaic: תָּא שְׁמַע, דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי:
phrases.english: Come and hear, as Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says:
One who sells his slave to a gentile —
phrases.notes: Refers to a Canaanite slave.

phrases.english: they penalize him up to one hundred times his value!
phrases.notes: Implies that the fine amounts are not exact limits.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע, דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to answer the question in step 5 with a case of a larger fine.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יהושע בן לוי's hundred-times fine for selling a slave to a גוי

steps.title: A slave is different because he loses מצוות daily
steps.stepSummary: The proof is rejected. A slave is a special case, because every day with the גוי he is kept from מצוות, so a bigger fine fits. 'Ten' for an animal can still be exact.
steps.simpleTranslation: A slave is different, because every single day he is removed from מצוות.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof. The slave case is more serious than the animal case, so its higher fine does not show that the animal's 'ten' is inexact.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An עבד כנעני is obligated in some מצוות. Under a גוי owner he cannot keep them, and that harm repeats every day. That explains the hundred-times fine. It says nothing about selling an animal, where ten may still be the true limit.

keyTerms.meaning: It is different. Separates one case from another

phrases.english: A slave is different,
as each and every day
the gentile removes him from מצוות.
phrases.notes: The ongoing daily loss of מצוות justifies a harsher fine.

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁאנֵי עֶבֶד, דְּכׇל יוֹמָא וְיוֹמָא מַפְקַע לֵיהּ מִמִּצְוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of step 6 by showing that the slave case is unique.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects using the slave fine to show that the animal fine of 'ten' is not exact
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The slave case is harsher because of the daily loss of מצוות, so it cannot be compared to an animal
steps.whatToRemember: A higher fine for selling a slave does not prove that the animal's ten-times fine is inexact. A slave is a special case because he loses מצוות every day. So the question of דוקא stays unresolved here.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the size of a rabbinic קנס can depend on how serious the ongoing harm is.

steps.title: Second version: ריש לקיש says up to one hundred times
steps.stepSummary: In the איכא דאמרי version, ריש לקיש fines a person who sells a large animal to a גוי up to one hundred times its value.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say a different version: ריש לקיש said that one who sells a large animal to a non-Jew is fined up to one hundred times its value.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now gives a second version of ריש לקיש's statement. In this version the fine is one hundred times, not ten.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first version said 'up to ten times.' This version raises the number to one hundred. Everything that follows next is built on this new number.

keyTerms.meaning: And some say: this introduces a second version of a teaching
A large animal, such as a cow or donkey
We fine him: the רבנן impose a penalty
Up to one hundred times its value

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new argument. It is the same ריש לקיש ruling in a different version, with the number one hundred instead of ten.

phrases.english: And there are those who say (a different version):
Reish Lakish said:
One who sells a large animal to a non-Jew,
we fine him up to one hundred times its value.
phrases.notes: He must buy it back from the non-Jew, even at a high price.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second version of the ריש לקיש ruling from step 4, with a larger fine.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Selling a large animal to a גוי carries a fine of up to one hundred times its value.

steps.title: A ברייתא says only ten times for giving an animal in receivership
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא fines someone who gives his animal to a גוי in קבלנות only up to ten times, which seems to contradict one hundred.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned: one who gives it to him in receivership, even though he is not allowed to, is fined up to ten times its value.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges ריש לקיש's one hundred with a ברייתא that says ten.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both cases involve giving a large animal over to a גוי. If the ברייתא fines only ten times, why would ריש לקיש fine one hundred? The two numbers seem to clash.

keyTerms.meaning: We learned: introduces a cited source from the תנאים
In receivership: giving an animal to someone to raise in exchange for a share of the profits

phrases.english: We learned: and one who gives it to him in receivership,
even though he is not permitted to do so,
we fine him up to ten times its value!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the one-hundred figure from step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: ריש לקיש's fine of one hundred times.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא about a similar case sets the fine at only ten times.

steps.title: A sale cuts the animal off completely; receivership does not
steps.stepSummary: With a sale, the animal fully leaves the Jew's ownership. With קבלנות, it still belongs to him, so the fine is smaller.
steps.simpleTranslation: A sale cuts it off from him. Receivership does not cut it off from him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the two cases are different, so their fines can differ.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In a sale, the animal is gone from the Jew for good, so the fine is harsher (one hundred). In קבלנות, the Jew still owns the animal, so the fine is lighter (ten).

keyTerms.meaning: It is cut off from him: he no longer owns it

phrases.english: A sale: it is cut off from him;
receivership: it is not cut off from him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction raised in step 9.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Sale and receivership are the same, so the fines should match.
steps.terutzMaskana: A sale is a full loss of ownership and gets a heavier fine. Receivership keeps ownership and gets a lighter fine.

steps.title: Is one hundred an exact number?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether 'one hundred' is a precise limit or just a general expression.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is it exact, or not exact?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks whether ריש לקיש's 'one hundred' is a real, exact limit. This sets up the next move, a proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If 'one hundred' is exact, the fine stops there. If it is not exact, it may just mean 'a very large amount.'

phrases.english: Exactly, or not exactly?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Now that one hundred stands, the גמרא asks how literally to take it.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether one hundred is a fixed amount or just an expression.

steps.title: Proof attempt: a slave sold to a גוי gets only ten times
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן לוי fines the seller of a slave to a גוי only ten times, which suggests the numbers are not exact.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: רבי יהושע בן לוי said, one who sells his slave to a non-Jew is fined up to ten times his value.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to prove that 'one hundred' is not exact by bringing the slave case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Selling a slave seems at least as serious as selling an animal, because the slave loses מצוות. Yet the slave fine is only ten, while the animal fine is one hundred. That suggests these numbers are just loose expressions.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear: introduces a proof
His value (masculine, referring to the slave)

phrases.english: Come and hear:
For Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said:
One who sells his slave to a non-Jew,
we fine him up to ten times his value!

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע, דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to answer the question in step 11.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יהושע בן לוי's ten-times fine for selling a slave.

steps.title: A slave is different because he does not come back
steps.stepSummary: The proof is rejected. A slave bought back is set free and does not return to the owner, so his fine is smaller.
steps.simpleTranslation: A slave is different, because he does not return to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof by showing that the slave case is different from the animal case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the owner redeems the slave from the גוי, the slave goes free and does not come back to the owner. The owner already loses out, so the רבנן fined him less. That means the slave case does not prove that 'one hundred' is loose.

keyTerms.meaning: He does not return to him

phrases.english: A slave is different,
since he does not return to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in step 12.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The comparison between the slave and the animal.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The slave does not return to the owner after redemption, so a lower fine makes sense.

steps.title: If that is the reason, the animal fine should be only a little more
steps.stepSummary: If the only difference is that the animal returns to the owner, the animal fine should be only one unit higher (eleven), not one hundred.
steps.simpleTranslation: With an animal, what is the reason? Because it comes back to him? Then fine him only one more!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the rejection in step 13.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Getting the animal back is worth about one value, the animal itself. So that difference would explain at most eleven times, not a jump from ten to one hundred. The answer in step 13 does not explain such a big gap.

keyTerms.meaning: Let us fine him just one more

phrases.english: An animal, what is the reason (for the larger fine)?
Because it returns to him?
Then let us fine him only one more!
phrases.notes: That would be eleven times, not one hundred.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the distinction made in step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reason that a slave 'does not return.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: That difference is worth only one extra value, so it cannot explain a gap from ten to one hundred.

steps.title: Selling a slave is uncommon, so the רבנן did not decree strongly
steps.stepSummary: A new distinction: selling a slave to a גוי is rare, and the רבנן do not make decrees about rare cases. So the slave fine cannot be compared to the animal fine.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, a slave is an uncommon matter, and for any uncommon matter the רבנן did not make a decree.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops the earlier reason and gives a new one for why the slave case is different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Selling a slave to a גוי rarely happens, so the רבנן did not build a strong fine around it. Selling animals is common, so they set a heavy fine. Because the two cases follow different rules, the slave case cannot prove that 'one hundred' is not exact.

keyTerms.meaning: The רבנן did not make a decree about it

steps.whatToRemember: In the second version, ריש לקיש fines one hundred times for selling an animal. A sale is harsher than קבלנות (ten times). The slave case (ten times) does not prove that the number is loose, because selling a slave is uncommon and the רבנן do not make decrees about uncommon cases.
steps.whyThisMatters: The rule 'כל מילתא דלא שכיחא לא גזרו בה רבנן' appears across ש״ס. It explains why rabbinic decrees focus on common situations.

phrases.english: Rather, a slave
is an uncommon matter,
and any uncommon matter,
the Sages did not make a decree about it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא, עֶבֶד — מִילְּתָא דְלָא שְׁכִיחָא הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the reason rejected in step 14 with a new distinction.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The slave fine is smaller because the slave does not return to the owner.
steps.terutzMaskana: The slave fine follows a different rule because the case is uncommon, so it cannot prove anything about the animal fine.

steps.title: Both sides learn from the same verse
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings back the view of the חכמים in the ברייתא. רבי יהושע then says that both they and רבי יהודה learn their opinions from the same words, ״כׇּל בְּכוֹר״.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the חכמים say: as long as the גוי has a hand (a share) in the animal, etc. רבי יהושע said: both of them learned their view from one verse, ״כׇּל בְּכוֹר״ ('all the firstborn').
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the argument in the ברייתא and says that both opinions come from the same Torah verse. This sets up the next steps, which explain how each side reads it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה says that if a Jew owns part of the firstborn animal, his share is holy as a בכור. The חכמים say that if a גוי owns any part, there is no בכורה at all. רבי יהושע's point is that this is not a fight between two different sources. It is a fight over how to read one verse.

keyTerms.meaning: The 'hand' of the גוי, meaning his ownership share
They explained one and the same verse

steps.confusionAlert: This line is not a new ברייתא. The גמרא is re-quoting the חכמים from the ברייתא it already brought, so it can now explain where their view comes from.

phrases.english: And the Sages say:
As long as the gentile has a hand (ownership) in it, etc.
phrases.notes: Re-quoting the ברייתא from 2b

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua said:
And both of them expounded one verse,
"All the firstborn."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ: וּשְׁנֵיהֶם מִקְרָא אֶחָד דָּרְשׁוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the side discussion about fines and goes back to the ברייתא about an animal shared with a גוי.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יהודה and the חכמים both build their views on the same words, ״כׇּל בְּכוֹר״.

steps.title: First explanation: what the plain word 'firstborn' means
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים say the plain word ״בְּכוֹר״ would include even a partly owned animal, so ״כׇּל״ comes to require full Jewish ownership. רבי יהודה says the plain word means a fully owned animal, so ״כׇּל״ comes to include even a tiny Jewish share.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן hold: the word ״בְּכוֹר״ alone means even part of a firstborn. So the Torah wrote ״כׇּל״, meaning not until the whole animal is there (owned by a Jew). רבי יהודה holds: the word ״בְּכוֹר״ alone means a whole firstborn. So the Torah wrote ״כׇּל״, meaning even any amount.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how each side reads the verse. They disagree about what the plain word ״בְּכוֹר״ would mean if the Torah had not added ״כׇּל״.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sides agree that ״כׇּל״ changes the meaning of ״בְּכוֹר״. They disagree about the starting point. The חכמים: 'firstborn' alone means even a partial firstborn, so 'all' narrows it to a full one. רבי יהודה: 'firstborn' alone means a full firstborn, so 'all' widens it to even a small share.

keyTerms.meaning: All of it, the whole thing
Any amount at all, even a little

phrases.english: The Rabbis hold:
"Firstborn" implies even part of a firstborn;
the Merciful One wrote "all" —
meaning: not until the whole of it is there (Jewish-owned).
And Rabbi Yehuda holds:
"Firstborn" implies a whole firstborn;
the Merciful One wrote "all" —
meaning: even any amount at all.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the 'one verse' claim of רבי יהושע from Step 16.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For the חכמים, ״כׇּל״ requires the whole animal to be Jewish-owned. For רבי יהודה, ״כׇּל״ includes even a tiny Jewish share.

steps.title: Second explanation: both agree on 'firstborn', argue about 'all'
steps.stepSummary: Another way to explain it: everyone agrees that ״בְּכוֹר״ alone means majority ownership. The argument is whether ״כׇּל״ adds to that (requiring the whole animal) or takes away from it (allowing even a small share).
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, say instead: everyone agrees that ״בְּכוֹר״ alone means a majority. One Sage holds that ״כׇּל״ comes to add (fill it up to the whole). The other Sage holds that it comes to take away (allow even less than a majority).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second, different explanation of the same argument. This time both sides agree on the plain word and disagree only about what ״כׇּל״ does.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 17, the two sides disagreed about the meaning of ״בְּכוֹר״. Here they agree it means 'mostly owned.' The חכמים read ״כׇּל״ as pushing the requirement up to full ownership. רבי יהודה reads it as lowering the requirement to even a small share.

keyTerms.meaning: If you wish, say (an alternative explanation)

steps.confusionAlert: ״מָר סָבַר... וּמָר סָבַר״ does not say who is who. The first ('to fill') is the חכמים, and the second ('to reduce') is רבי יהודה.

phrases.english: If you wish, say:
that everyone agrees "firstborn" implies a majority;
one Sage holds: "all" implies it comes to fill out (to require the whole),
phrases.notes: The חכמים

phrases.english: and one Sage holds: it comes to reduce (to allow even less).
phrases.notes: רבי יהודה

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא, דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא ״בְּכוֹר״ רוּבָּא מַשְׁמַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different way to understand the same verse-based argument from Step 17.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Both sides agree that ״בְּכוֹר״ alone means majority ownership. ״כׇּל״ either raises the requirement to full ownership (חכמים) or lowers it to any share (רבי יהודה).

steps.title: How small can the gentile's share be?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: according to the חכמים, how big must the גוי's share be to cancel בכורה?
steps.simpleTranslation: And how much must the גוי's partnership be, so that the animal is exempt from בכורה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a practical question about the חכמים' view: what is the smallest share a גוי can own and still cancel בכורה? This sets up רב הונא's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חכמים said 'as long as the גוי has a hand in it.' This question asks how small that 'hand' can be. Does he need a real portion, or is even a tiny part enough?

keyTerms.meaning: Exempt from the laws of the firstborn

phrases.english: And how much must the gentile's partnership be,
for it to be exempt from firstborn status?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from where the views come from to the practical size of the גוי's share.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The smallest share a גוי can own and still cancel בכורה, according to the חכמים.

steps.title: רב הונא: even owning the ear is enough
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא answers that even if the גוי owns only the animal's ear, the animal is exempt from בכורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said: even its ear.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא answers the question: even a tiny share, like the ear, is enough to cancel בכורה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a very small amount. It takes the חכמים' phrase 'as long as the גוי has a hand in it' at its broadest: any real share at all cancels בכורה.

phrases.english: Rav Huna said:
Even its ear.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 19.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Even if the גוי owns just the ear, the animal is exempt from בכורה.

steps.title: רב נחמן: just let him take his ear and go
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן objects to רב הונא. If the גוי owns only the ear, the כהן can tell him, 'Take your ear and go,' and the rest of the animal should still be a בכור.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן challenged this: Let him (the כהן) say to him (the גוי), 'Take your ear and go!'
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן attacks רב הונא's answer. He argues that such a tiny share should not be able to cancel בכורה for the whole animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the גוי owns only the ear, his share can easily be separated. The ear can be cut off and handed to him, and the כהן keeps the rest. So why should the ear cancel בכורה for the whole animal? The objection suggests the גוי's share must be something that cannot simply be removed.

keyTerms.meaning: He challenged it (raised a strong objection)

steps.confusionAlert: Cutting off the ear blemishes the animal. That is not a problem here, because a blemished בכור still belongs to the כהן and he may eat it.

phrases.english: Rav Naḥman objects to this:
But let him (the priest) say to him (the gentile):
"Take your ear and go!"

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב הונא's answer from Step 20.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's rule that owning just the ear cancels בכורה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A share as small as the ear can be cut off and given to the גוי, so it should not cancel the holiness of the rest of the animal.

steps.title: רב חסדא and רבא: the share must be a vital body part
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא says the גוי's share must be a part whose removal makes the animal a נבלה. רבא says a part whose removal makes it a טריפה is enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: רב חסדא says the share must be a body part that would make the animal a נבלה. רבא says it must be a body part that would make it a טריפה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new view on how big the גוי's share must be. Unlike רב הונא's ear, the share must be a part the animal needs in order to live.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both אמוראים avoid רב נחמן's problem. The כהן cannot say 'take your part and go' when that part is essential to the animal's life. They disagree on how essential it must be. For רב חסדא, losing it must cause death right away (נבלה). For רבא, it is enough if losing it makes the animal a טריפה.

keyTerms.meaning: It was stated (introduces a dispute between אמוראים)
Here: an animal that dies right away when this part is removed
An animal with a fatal defect that will not survive in the long run
A body part whose removal makes the animal…

steps.confusionAlert: In this context, נבלה does not mean an animal that was slaughtered wrongly. It means a body part so vital that the animal dies right away without it.

phrases.english: It was stated: Rav Chisda says:
a part that makes it a carcass (dies immediately without it),
and Rava says:
a part that makes it a tereifa.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different answer to the question of Step 19, one that avoids רב נחמן's objection to רב הונא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The גוי's share cancels בכורה only if it is a vital part. רב חסדא requires a part that causes נבלה. רבא accepts even a part that causes טריפה.

steps.title: What is the root of their disagreement?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what principle רב חסדא and רבא disagree about.
steps.simpleTranslation: About what do they disagree?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the reason behind the dispute between רב חסדא and רבא. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both agree that the part must be vital. The question is why רבא counts a טריפה-causing part as vital and רב חסדא does not.

phrases.english: About what do they disagree?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind the dispute in Step 22.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The underlying principle that separates רב חסדא from רבא.

steps.title: They argue whether a טריפה can live
steps.stepSummary: רבא holds that a טריפה cannot live, so a part that causes טריפה is truly vital. רב חסדא holds that a טריפה can live, so only a part that causes נבלה counts.
steps.simpleTranslation: They disagree about whether a טריפה can live. The one who says 'a part that makes it a טריפה' holds that a טריפה cannot live. The one who says 'a part that makes it a נבלה' holds that a טריפה can live.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the whole dispute depends on one question: can a טריפה animal survive?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The share must be a part the animal cannot live without. If a טריפה cannot live (רבא), then a part whose loss causes טריפה is already a life-or-death part. If a טריפה can live (רב חסדא), the animal could survive without that part, so only a part whose loss causes immediate death is enough.

keyTerms.meaning: According to the one who says

steps.whyThisMatters: This links the בכורה question to a well-known general dispute about whether a טריפה can live.

phrases.english: About whether a tereifa can live.

phrases.aramaic: לְמַאן דְּאָמַר דָּבָר שֶׁעוֹשֶׂה אוֹתוֹ טְרֵיפָה —
phrases.english: According to the one who says 'a part that makes it a tereifa' —
he holds a tereifa cannot live,

phrases.aramaic: וּלְמַאן דְּאָמַר דָּבָר שֶׁעוֹשֶׂה אוֹתוֹ נְבֵלָה —
phrases.english: and according to the one who says 'a part that makes it a carcass' —
but a tereifa can live.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 23.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: They disagree whether a טריפה can live. רבא says it cannot, and רב חסדא says it can.

steps.title: Proposal: רב הונא speaks of the firstborn, the others of the mother
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן suggest to רב פפא that רב הונא does not argue with רב חסדא and רבא. רב הונא's ear ruling is about the firstborn itself, and their vital-part ruling is about the mother.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן said before רב פפא: רב הונא, and רב חסדא and רבא, do not disagree. This ruling is about the firstborn itself, and that ruling is about its mother.
steps.whatsHappening: The רבנן try to make peace between רב הונא and רב חסדא/רבא. They say the rulings cover two different cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to this proposal, if the גוי owns even an ear of the firstborn itself, it is exempt (רב הונא). If the גוי owns a share of the mother, that share only counts if it is a vital part (רב חסדא and רבא). This way, both rulings can be true.

phrases.english: The Sages said it before Rav Pappa:

phrases.aramaic: הָא דְּרַב הוּנָא, וְרַב חִסְדָּא וְרָבָא —
phrases.english: that of Rav Huna, and Rav Chisda and Rava —
do not disagree;
this is about it (the firstborn), that is about its mother.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to reconcile רב הונא (Step 20) with רב חסדא and רבא (Step 22).
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): firstborn itself versus its mother
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב הונא and רב חסדא/רבא seem to argue about how big the share must be.
steps.terutzMaskana: They talk about different cases, so there is no argument.

steps.title: רב פפא: the same ״כׇּל״ applies to the mother
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא rejects the split. If ownership of the firstborn must be complete because of ״כׇּל בְּכוֹר״, then ownership of the mother must also be complete because of ״כׇּל מִקְנְךָ תִּזָּכָר״.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said to them: Why would the firstborn be different? Because we need 'all the firstborn,' and that is missing? For the mother we also need 'all your livestock,' and that is missing too!
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא attacks the proposal to split the cases. He shows that the reason given for the firstborn applies just as strongly to the mother.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The only reason a tiny share in the firstborn should cancel בכורה is the word ״כׇּל״, which requires full Jewish ownership. But the פסוק about the mother, ״כׇּל מִקְנְךָ״, also says ״כׇּל״. So a tiny share in the mother should count the same way. The split between the two cases has no basis.

keyTerms.meaning: 'All your livestock that is male' (שמות ל״ד:י״ט)

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said to them:
What is different about it (the firstborn)?
That we require 'all the firstborn' and it is not there?
For its mother too we require
'all your livestock that is male,' and it is not there!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהוּ רַב פָּפָּא: מַאי שְׁנָא בּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the reconciliation proposed in Step 25.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole split between the firstborn and the mother.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The word ״כׇּל״ appears for the mother just as it does for the firstborn, so the two cases have the same rule.

steps.title: No difference: the dispute stands in both cases
steps.stepSummary: Since there is no difference between the firstborn and the mother, רב הונא really does argue with רב חסדא and רבא in both cases.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, there is no difference.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא finishes his rejection and concludes that the split fails. The firstborn and the mother follow the same rule, so the dispute is real.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב הונא holds that even an ear is enough, for both the firstborn and the mother. רב חסדא and רבא require a vital part, for both the firstborn and the mother. The attempt to make peace between them is withdrawn.
steps.whatToRemember: How big must the גוי's share be? רב הונא says even an ear is enough. רב חסדא says it must be a part whose loss kills the animal right away (נבלה). רבא says a part whose loss makes it a טריפה is enough, because a טריפה cannot live. This dispute applies equally to a share in the firstborn and a share in its mother, since ״כׇּל״ appears in both פסוקים.

phrases.english: Rather, there is no difference.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion from רב פפא's rejection in Step 26.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The firstborn and the mother are treated the same, so רב הונא truly disagrees with רב חסדא and רבא in both cases.

steps.title: Why are non-viable newborns different?
steps.stepSummary: מר בר רב אשי asks: נפלים cannot live, yet they are holy as a בכור. So why does a gentile's share in a vital part exempt the animal?
steps.simpleTranslation: מר בר רב אשי challenged this: How is this different from נפלים? They cannot survive, yet they are still holy. As the master said: ״פֶּטֶר שֶׁגֶר בְּהֵמָה״ teaches that anything that dwelled inside the animal is included.
steps.whatsHappening: מר בר רב אשי attacks the vital-part ruling. If being unable to live does not stop בכורה for נפלים, then making the animal unable to live should not stop it here either.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב חסדא and רבא said that if a gentile owns a part whose removal would make the animal unable to live, the animal is exempt. But a פסוק teaches that even נפלים, which cannot live at all, are holy as a בכור. So 'unable to live' does not seem to be a reason for exemption.

keyTerms.meaning: He challenged it (a strong objection to a statement)
The opening of an animal's womb (״שגר״ is read as 'what dwells inside')

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read ״שֶׁגֶר״ here as a simple word for 'womb'. The דרשה reads it as 'whatever dwelled inside the animal', and that is why even נפלים are included.

phrases.aramaic: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ מָר בַּר רַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Mar bar Rav Ashi challenged it:
How is this different from non-viable newborns,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאַף עַל גַּב דְּלָאו בְּנֵי חִיּוּתָא נִינְהוּ קָדְשִׁי,
phrases.english: which, even though they cannot live, are holy,
as the master said: "The firstborn that emerges from [sheger] an animal"
phrases.notes: שמות י״ג:י״ב

phrases.english: means: whatever dwelled inside the animal!
phrases.notes: This includes even a non-viable fetus.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ מָר בַּר רַב אָשֵׁי: מַאי שְׁנָא מִנְּפָלִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After establishing that רב הונא argues with רב חסדא and רבא, the גמרא challenges the reasoning behind רב חסדא and רבא's vital-part ruling.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling of רב חסדא and רבא that a gentile's share in a vital part exempts the animal from בכורה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: נפלים cannot live, yet they are holy as a בכור, so the inability to live cannot be the reason for exemption.

steps.title: Mixed non-holy ownership is the real problem
steps.stepSummary: With נפלים, nothing non-holy is mixed in, so ״כׇּל בְּכוֹר״ applies. Here, the gentile's share mixes in non-holy ownership, so ״כׇּל בְּכוֹר״ does not apply.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, with נפלים, since nothing non-holy is mixed in, we apply ״כׇּל בְּכוֹר״ to the animal. Here, since non-holy ownership is mixed in, we do not apply ״כׇּל בְּכוֹר״.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The reason for exemption is not that the animal cannot live. The reason is that part of it belongs to a gentile.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A נפל is entirely Jewish-owned, so the whole thing is holy, even though it cannot survive. When a gentile owns a vital part, a non-holy share is mixed in, and the word ״כׇּל״ (all) requires the בכור to be completely holy. The vital part matters only because it makes the gentile's share count for the whole animal.

keyTerms.meaning: Non-holy (חולין) ownership is mixed into them
We apply the verse to them

steps.whatToRemember: Not being able to live does not cancel בכורה, as we see from נפלים. Mixed gentile ownership cancels it, because ״כׇּל בְּכוֹר״ requires the בכור to be fully holy.

phrases.aramaic: הָתָם, כֵּיוָן דְּלָא עָרִיבוּ בְּהוּ חוּלִּין —
phrases.english: There, since nothing non-holy is mixed in with them,
we apply to the animal "all the firstborn,"
here, since something non-holy is mixed in with them,
we do not apply to them "all the firstborn."

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם, כֵּיוָן דְּלָא עָרִיבוּ בְּהוּ חוּלִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: This answers מר בר רב אשי's challenge by separating the two cases.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases (חילוק): viability versus mixed ownership
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The exemption seemed to come from the animal being unable to live, which would clash with the law of נפלים.
steps.terutzMaskana: The exemption comes from the gentile's share, which mixes in non-holy ownership and blocks ״כׇּל בְּכוֹר״. נפלים have no such mix.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר asks what was taught in the בית המדרש
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר missed the בית המדרש, met רבי אסי, and asked him what the חכמים had said there. רבי אסי begins to answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר did not go into the בית המדרש. He found רבי אסי and asked him: What did the חכמים say in the בית המדרש? רבי אסי said to him:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a short story to introduce a new teaching. This line is only a setup. רבי אסי's actual report comes in the next part.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No ruling is given here yet. The story frame tells us that what comes next is a report of a discussion in the בית המדרש, which רבי אלעזר will then respond to.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר לָא עַל לְבֵי מִדְרְשָׁא,
phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar did not enter the study hall,
he found Rabbi Asi,

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מַאי אֲמוּר רַבָּנַן בֵּי מִדְרְשָׁא?
phrases.english: and said to him: What did the Sages say in the study hall?
He said to him:
phrases.notes: The answer continues on the next amud.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר לָא עַל לְבֵי מִדְרְשָׁא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After closing the challenge about נפלים, the גמרא moves to a new report from the בית המדרש.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the חכמים taught in the בית המדרש while רבי אלעזר was absent
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Not yet given. רבי אסי's report follows on the next amud.
